oil.summary: Crude markets are under severe pressure, with WTI settling at $80.47/bbl (-5.20%) and Brent at $83.12/bbl (-4.82%), extending a bruising month that has erased more than 20% from both benchmarks. The dominant driver today is the US-Iran preliminary agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, confirmed by an LNG tanker successfully transiting the chokepoint for the first time since the deal was announced. Markets are pricing in a meaningful supply-risk premium unwind, though analysts caution that a swift restoration of Iranian oil and gas flows is not guaranteed. Options markets reflect the bearish skew, with CME OPEC Watch assigning a 77.26% probability to a production increase at the next meeting. Countering the downside somewhat, Ukraine's intensified drone campaign against Russian refinery infrastructure and Russia's consequent decision to ease environmental fuel standards signal tightening domestic Russian supply, though this is insufficient to offset the Hormuz relief rally reversal.
drivers: US-Iran preliminary deal and first LNG tanker clearing Strait of Hormuz triggers large geopolitical risk-premium unwind, sending WTI and Brent down ~5% on the day
CME OPEC Watch pricing 77.26% probability of a production increase at the next meeting, amplifying bearish sentiment
Ukraine drone strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and Russia easing fuel-quality standards signal internal Russian supply stress, providing only marginal downside offset

gas.summary: European and US natural gas markets are diverging sharply. TTF collapsed 10.25% to 41.98 €/MWh on the day, continuing a steep 15.75% weekly decline, as the Hormuz reopening raises expectations of resumed LNG flows into Europe and Asia from the Gulf. Henry Hub, by contrast, edged up 0.90% to $3.148/MMBtu, sustaining a solid month-on-month gain of 8.78%, insulated from the Hormuz narrative by domestic supply-demand dynamics. A potential supply disruption at Inpex's 9.2-mtpa Ichthys LNG facility in Australia remains live after the Fair Work Commission denied an employer request to block a strike, which could tighten Asian spot LNG supply and partially offset European relief from Hormuz reopening. The Russia fuel-quality story is a gas-adjacent negative for European energy security assumptions, though the headline impact today is dwarfed by the Hormuz development.
drivers: Hormuz reopening and first successful LNG transit crush TTF by more than 10% as European market prices in restored Gulf LNG availability
Australian Fair Work Commission clears an Inpex Ichthys LNG strike, introducing near-term supply risk for Asian buyers that could redirect spot cargoes away from Europe
Henry Hub outperforms, up 0.90% on the day and +8.78% month-on-month, reflecting domestic US fundamentals largely decoupled from the Hormuz-driven sell-off

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs bucked the broader energy sell-off, gaining 3.46% to $75.575/EUA, extending a weekly rise of 3.72% and a monthly gain of 6.65%. The move is notable given that TTF's sharp 10.25% decline should theoretically reduce gas-to-coal switching incentives and lower carbon demand from the power sector; the EUA rally therefore suggests structural buying or compliance-driven demand is overriding short-term fuel-price signals. On the structural side, India's solar capacity is forecast to grow 22% annually through 2035 driven by data-centre power demand per a Nuvama report, while New Delhi is simultaneously pushing states to fast-track nuclear and battery storage approvals, signalling a broadening of the energy mix beyond renewables. The Iran deal and Hormuz reopening are primarily an oil and LNG story for power markets, with second-order effects on European generation costs likely to materialise only as TTF softness feeds through to gas-fired dispatch economics.
drivers: EU carbon EUAs rally 3.46% despite falling gas prices, suggesting compliance or structural buying is dominating short-term fuel-switching logic
India's solar capacity projected at 22% annual growth to 2035, with federal government accelerating nuclear and battery storage approvals, underlining long-run demand transformation
Hormuz reopening and TTF collapse create a lagged downward pressure on European gas-fired power generation costs, but direct power-market impact is not yet reflected in today's carbon price action
